recent_posts.title: Code Reviewing My Own Game Engine Series (Hazel 2D)
recent_posts.summary: A code review of the Hazel 2D game engine series codebase, originally started in 2018. The author walks through the public GitHub repo, examining architecture decisions including the layer system, event system, static singletons, renderer abstraction, 2D batched rendering with SPIR-V shaders, ECS, C# scripting via Mono, and ImGui integration. Key criticisms include overuse of static/global state, poor lifetime management, a too-fine-grained renderer abstraction, and missing features like prefabs and a runtime executable. The author considers starting a new engine from scratch using AI assistance to handle boilerplate while focusing on architecture and design, potentially as a new YouTube series.

recent_posts.title: Hazel game engine renderer rewritten using NVRHI graphics abstraction layer
recent_posts.summary: The Hazel game engine's Renderer 2025 overhaul is complete and merged into the main dev branch. The core change replaces Hazel's custom Vulkan-only abstraction layer with NVIDIA's NVRHI (Rendering Hardware Interface), which abstracts Vulkan, D3D11, and D3D12 backends. This shifts maintenance of the graphics API abstraction to Nvidia's library while Hazel retains a fork for custom patches. The change improves cross-GPU vendor compatibility (notably AMD) and reduces internal maintenance burden. Shader pipeline abstraction across APIs remains incomplete, as NVRHI doesn't handle shader compilation. Dear ImGui was also upgraded to a much newer version as part of this effort.

recent_posts.title: Dangling pointers from temporary std::string objects in C++
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into a subtle C++ bug involving dangling pointers from temporary std::string objects. When a function returns a std::string by value and you immediately call .c_str() on it, the pointer is only valid within the same expression. Storing that pointer in a variable and using it on the next line is undefined behavior because the temporary string is destroyed at the end of the statement. The video demonstrates this with GCC, Clang, and MSVC, showing how the bug can silently appear to work depending on compiler, optimization level, and memory state. The safe fix is to store the string in a named variable before extracting a char pointer, making the lifetime explicit.

recent_posts.title: Reference Counting in C++
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into intrusive reference counting in C++, using the Hazel game engine's custom `Ref` class as a practical example. Explains how reference counting tracks object lifetimes by incrementing/decrementing a counter on copy/destruction, deleting the underlying heap object when the count reaches zero. Contrasts this approach with `std::shared_ptr`, which uses non-intrusive reference counting (storing the count externally), and `std::enable_shared_from_this`, which is the closest standard-library analog but still not truly intrusive. A multi-threaded example demonstrates why intrusive reference counting is especially useful when multiple threads share ownership of a resource and the last user is unpredictable. The key advantage of intrusive reference counting is that the count lives inside the object itself, enabling safe self-referential shared ownership without external control blocks.

recent_posts.title: Avoiding use after delete bugs when destroying objects from within their own methods
recent_posts.summary: Deleting an object while still executing its member function is a subtle but dangerous bug in C++. When transitioning between application layers, reassigning a unique_ptr in a vector can destroy the current layer object while its on_update method is still on the call stack. This creates undefined behavior that may not crash immediately but can corrupt memory or cause security vulnerabilities. The solution is to queue transitions and execute them at safe synchronization points (like end-of-frame) rather than immediately during execution. Using tools like address sanitizer and understanding call stacks helps identify these lifetime issues.

recent_posts.title: HTTP SERVER in C++
recent_posts.summary: A practical walkthrough of building an HTTP server in C++ using the httplib header-only library. The tutorial demonstrates setting up a VPS, compiling C++ code remotely via SSH, and creating a functional web server that serves content over HTTP. The guide emphasizes simplicity by avoiding complex build systems, showing how to use a single-header library with minimal setup to handle HTTP requests and serve files from a remote server.

top_posts.title: 11-year-old builds a game engine: code review and advice
top_posts.summary: An 11-year-old named Anthony submitted his game engine project, 'Real Engine,' for a code review by Chenno. Despite being so young, Anthony managed to include a README, license, and instructions for his project. Chenno engages with the code, providing constructive feedback and corrections, particularly focusing on issues with precompiled headers and shader management. The post also highlights the importance of separating external dependencies into static libraries. Additionally, Chenno introduces the use of AI in code reviews through Code Rabbit, which can help in identifying potential bugs and improving code structure.

top_posts.title: C++ Application Architecture - A Mini-Series
top_posts.summary: A comprehensive guide to architecting C++ applications using a modular approach that separates core reusable systems from application-specific code. The tutorial demonstrates building a clean architecture with an application system, window management, main loop, and layer-based functionality using OpenGL. Key concepts include creating a core static library for reusable components, implementing a layer system for custom behavior, and maintaining clean separation between framework code and application logic. The approach emphasizes simplicity and reusability, making it easier to create multiple applications without reimplementing core functionality.

top_posts.title: C++23 introduces std::println function for simplified output
top_posts.summary: C++23 introduces a new std::println function that simplifies output operations, moving away from the traditional iostream approach. This change brings C++ closer to the printing syntax found in languages like Java and C#, making "Hello World" programs more straightforward to write.

top_posts.title: How C++ references become invalid when containers reallocate memory
top_posts.summary: References in C++ are syntactic sugar over pointers and point to specific memory addresses. When containers like vectors reallocate memory during operations like push_back, existing references become invalid and point to freed memory, causing crashes or undefined behavior. This applies to const references, string_view, and any reference to elements within dynamic data structures. Safer alternatives include using indices or getter functions that return fresh references on each call.

top_posts.title: In-Depth Code Review of a 13-Year-Old's C-Based Vulkan Graphics Engine
top_posts.summary: A code review of a graphics engine written in C using the Vulkan API by a 13-year-old programmer.
